title: Reducing exposure to indoor air pollution in

paragraphs.text: Cooking on a cleaner fuel The most effective means of reducing indoor air pollution is to switch from biomass* to cleaner fuel that produces significantly lower emissions. For those who are able to switch to fuels such as kerosene or Liquified Petroleum Gas (LPG), the benefits are great. In many urban areas these fuels cost less per unit than biomass. However, there is often a larger initial investment needed to purchase the fuels and the stoves. For example, LPG must be purchased each week or month by the cylinder, but many people can only afford to get a little fuel daily. Making fuel available in smaller units would benefit poorer customers. In rural areas there is less incentive to switch fuels, as biomass is gathered at no financial cost to the user.

Another alternative fuel, biogas, is extremely effective, as it converts a renewable material (dung and other organic waste materials) into a gaseous, clean fuel. While biogas is being introduced in parts of Asia very successfully-there are over 120,000 biogas plants in Nepal alone-traditional attitudes in other regions make it harder to introduce.

Getting smoke out of the house For those trapped into using biomass as their main domestic fuel for the foreseeable future, options for reducing exposure to indoor air pollution will entail safe ways of getting smoke out of the home.

Substantial reductions to smoke exposure have been obtained with relatively simple methods. For example, one project in Kenya reduced particulate and carbon monoxide pollution in homes by nearly 80% through the use of smoke hoods. These work on the same principle as chimneys but have the advantage of being freestanding and independent of the stove. Substantial benefits were also achieved by increasing the roof spaces in traditional houses and installing better-fitting doors. However, the enlargement of windows in the same project seemed to have little impact.

Cutting smoke volumes in improved biomass stoves Improved stoves were primarily designed to increase energy efficiency. The Upesi stove, incorporates a chimney, one would anticipate smoke would be reduced. There are some very effective chimney stoves which, when tested in the home, show a significant reduction in smoke. Good examples are the rocket stove and Ecostove, which are increasingly being used in Central America.

However, there are also potential problems with many chimney stoves: they may not perform well if they are not installed properly, or are poorly designed. Chimneys are expensive and may be ineffective if the smoke returns through doors and windows. They can also block up quickly with soot and require regular cleaning.

Reducing the need for fire A very simple technology can reduce the need for fuel for cooking- this is the fireless cooker, or ‘hay box’. This acts like a slow cooker, and is good for making soups, rice or stews. The food is heated to boiling, then placed in a box filled with insulating material, such as hay or crumpled newspaper. The food continues to cook slowly. The development organization Winrock found that the hay box was in demand with women’s groups in Nairobi, where they are proving as popular as improved stoves.

As much of the need for improved cooking comes from countries with abundant sunshine, it would seem a logical step to move towards solar power, and there are some passionate advocates for this technology. Solar cookers, which concentrate sunlight directly to cook food, have been seen as a clean, alternative way of cooking. Unfortunately there has been limited success in practices. The use of solar energy means preparing a meal at midday, which does not coincide with the main family mealtime in many cultures. It also requires the cook to work outdoors.

Changing patterns of behaviour Simple changes in the way the cook behaves can reduce exposure to smoke. For example, making sure that fuel wood is dry cuts emissions. The use of a pot lid can reduce the fuel consumed during simmering by a factor of three, and overall emission levels by almost a half. On the other hand, keeping children away from the fire may seem an obvious way of reducing their exposure, but as many children are habitually carried on their mother’s back, this can be very difficult, especially where the mother is the only childminder. Cooking outdoors would also reduce exposure to indoor air pollution, and in some parts of the world, for example amongst the aborigines in Australia, this is standard practice. However, for most cultures, cooking indoors is standard.

Identifying appropriate solutions Experience has indicated that there is no point trying to dictate a solution to a community. This is a view supported by a World Health Organization and US aid-supported consultation on indoor air pollution and health: ‘A single-issue, technology-driven approach to indoor air quality is doomed to failure…Such an approach frequently demands changes of the local community that affect numerous aspects of their lives.’ The authors argue that ‘the key to success is to adopt project approaches that broaden the range of secure and sustainable choices available locally, and thus enable people to devise their own solutions’.
